t: Tamil is a Dravidian language attested since about 300 BCE in Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions, and one of the longest-surviving classical languages in the world.

Its early literature includes the Tolkāppiyam, the oldest Tamil grammar, and the 2,381 Sangam poems, dated between the 1st century BCE and the 5th century CE; Tamil inscriptions have been found as far away as Sri Lanka, Thailand and Egypt.

Old Tamil became Middle Tamil by the 8th century and Modern Tamil from 1600; today Tamil is official in Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Sri Lanka and Singapore, and in 2004 it became the first recognised classical language of India.
dyk: Scholars trace the English word rice to Tamil arici, through loans from the Tamil of 400 BCE into Hebrew and then into Greek óruza.
ev: Old Tamil appears in short inscriptions in Tamil-Brahmi, a variant of the Brahmi script
The Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela, king of Kalinga, names a Tamira Samghatta, a Tamil confederacy
Egyptian pottery of this date found at Quseir al-Qadim, likely the port of Myos Hormos, bears Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions
Old Tamil has become Middle Tamil, which has gained a present tense and all but lost the old āytam sound
The Naṉṉūl restates the rules of the Tolkāppiyam and becomes the standard grammar of literary Tamil
Portuguese missionaries print the prayer book Thambiran Vanakkam, making Tamil the first Indian language to be printed and published
The Pure Tamil Movement campaigns to remove Sanskrit elements from Tamil
Tamil becomes the first legally recognised classical language of India

f.family: Dravidian, southern branch; descended from Proto-Dravidian, most likely spoken around the third millennium BCE. Its closest major relative is Malayalam, which began to diverge around the 9th century CE.
f.script: Tamil-Brahmi in its earliest inscriptions; later vaṭṭeḻuttu, alongside Grantha and Pallava, until the present Tamil script: 12 vowels, 18 consonants and the āytam, 247 characters in all, with six Grantha letters for borrowed sounds.
f.earliest: Short inscriptions in Tamil-Brahmi, attested since c. 300 BCE; earlier dates are claimed for writing on burial urns at Adichanallur (from at least 696 BCE) and a Keezhadi sample (around 580 BCE). The earliest long text is the Tolkāppiyam, whose oldest layers may date to the late 2nd century BCE.
f.status: Living: spoken by the Tamil people in Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and northern and eastern Sri Lanka and by communities worldwide; official in Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, an official language of Sri Lanka and Singapore, and in 2004 the first recognised classical language of India.
